title: ICLR 2025 - reading notes and takeaways
content:
Quick notes from ICLR 2025 (San Diego) - focus on sessions re: fast attention, memory/KV cache, compiler/kernel selection, and evals for inference quality. Mostly rough; TODOs at the end.

Sessions I cared about: 
- Fast sparse/dense attention tricks (paper: "Sparse Mixture Attention for Long Contexts", arXiv:2503.01234) - key idea: dynamically selecting attention heads to skip focusing on low-signal tokens. Results show 2-3x throughput improvement at similar perplexity on long-context tasks. Implementation notes: authors used custom CUDA kernels + fallback to Triton for small batches.
- Kernel autotuning papers + talk: autotune per-model/per-seqlen kernel selector. Important for us: exposes tradeoffs between throughput and latency across different seqlen distributions. They had a tiny profiling daemon that samples real traffic and updates kernel policy. Feels directly applicable to Redwood Optimize.
- KV cache compression (poster): lossy compression of KV states for cold items; aggressive quantization for long-tail tokens. Nice for Dedicated / Private when memory becomes a limiter.

Takeaways and items relevant to Redwood: 
1) Kernel selection + profiling fabric: build a lightweight offline sampler from production traces (sampling by route/model/seq len) to recommend kernels/tiling configs. Should be integrated into Optimize and Serving runtime policy. Link to demo repo in talk slides (github link above).
2) Quantization beyond 4-bit: mixed per-layer strategies + per-head rounding. Paper shows that per-head quantization can save 10-20% more without large quality regressions. Need to run on our in-house eval prompts to validate.
3) Streaming + prefix caching: interesting heuristic for early-exit attention on prefixes when later tokens are unlikely to change earlier distribution. Could reduce KV cache pressure for chat workloads.
4) Eval methodology: sessions emphasized multi-metric evals - e.g., latency-percentiles + task-specific metrics (QA F1 / Rouge / helpfulness). Idea: tie regressions to a small suite of prompts (we already do this) but expand to include long-context synthetic prompts and model-failure cases (tokenization edge-cases).

Notes-to-self / experiments to run: 
- Prototype tiny kernel-probing daemon: sample 1% of requests (low overhead), run microbenchmarks on representative batches to compare candidate kernels. Target: proof-of-concept in 2 weeks. (owner: Omar)
- Run per-head quantization experiment on mixtral/guanaco forks in staging (owner: Sophie). Use our eval harness and report delta on perplexity + chat quality.
- Add long-context prompts to canary evals (owner: Evelyn). Aim to detect KV cache regressions and prefix-related degradations.

Open questions / worries: 
- Stability of autotuned kernels across hardware generations (A100 -> H100 -> upcoming accelerators). Need to ensure policies degrade gracefully and do not cause noisy rollouts.
- Safety of lossy KV compression on safety-critical contexts - might change outputs subtly. Must flag as opt-in and add post-change checks.

References / useful links I scribbled down: 
- Sparse Mixture Attention for Long Contexts - arXiv:2503.01234 
- Fast-attention kernels demo repo: https://github.com/example/fast-attention (clone + run microbenchmarks)
- Slides: https://iclr2025.org/slides/session12 (poster + talk PDFs)
- Slack thread where I discussed this briefly: #eng-serving-runtime (see thread pinned May 11)

Meeting notes / follow-ups: 
- Sync with Sophie this week to prioritize per-head quantization experiments.
- Draft a short proposal for an autotune daemon and present in eng-applied-ml sync (due 2025-05-20).

Random scribbles: 
- Possible Linear ticket names: ML-kerneled-autotune, ML-kv-compress-optin, EVAL-long-context-suite.
- Quick perf numbers observed in talk: 2x throughput @ 1% perplexity delta for long contexts (kinda optimistic but promising).

END - informal scratchpad. Will formalize into a short PRD if experiments look good.
